Canada's Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentive program is the largest federal source of financial support for industrial research and innovation in the country, with industry analyses of Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) program statistics indicating approximately $4.6 billion in Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) allowed across 23,677 claims in the 2025–2026 fiscal period. Administered by the CRA under the statutory authority of the federal Income Tax Act (ITA), R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), and the Income Tax Regulations (ITR), C.R.C., c. 945, the program operates through a dual-pillar legislative architecture: (1) an immediate or indefinitely carryforwardable deduction against business income via the Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures under Section 37 of the ITA, and (2) a rate-differentiated Investment Tax Credit under Sections 127 and 127.1 of the ITA that provides an enhanced 35% credit (100% refundable on current expenditures and 40% refundable on capital expenditures up to an annual expenditure limit) for eligible Canadian corporations, or a 15% basic credit for other claimants.

Between December 2024 and October 2026, Canada's federal and provincial R&D tax regimes underwent their most expansive statutory overhaul in more than a decade. Federally, Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, enacted sweeping legislative amendments applicable to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (that is, on or after December 16, 2024). Bill C-15 doubled the maximum annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% ITC from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000 (increasing the maximum annual cash refund on current expenditures from $1,050,000 to $2,100,000), widened the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from the former $10,000,000–$50,000,000 range to a broader $15,000,000–$75,000,000 range, extended eligibility for the 35% refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) using a three-year average annual revenue phase-out test ($15,000,000–$75,000,000), and restored the eligibility of depreciable capital property, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and equipment lease expenditures acquired or incurred after December 15, 2024. Operationally, on April 1, 2026, the CRA launched an Optional Pre-Claim Approval Process using Form T1322, enabling eligible businesses with gross business income under $25,000,000 to secure upfront technical eligibility determinations within eight weeks and cutting post-filing expenditure review service standards in half from 180 calendar days to 90 calendar days.

Concurrently, major Canadian provinces restructured their complementary R&D tax credit frameworks. In Québec, for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, the provincial government abolished eight legacy innovation tax credits and consolidated them into the new Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) (Crédit d'impôt pour la recherche, l'innovation et la commercialisation), which provides a 30% fully refundable tax credit on the first $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures exceeding an applicable exclusion threshold and 20% on the excess, while expanding eligible activities to cover pre-commercialization regulatory validation and product design. In British Columbia, Bill 2 (Budget Measures Implementation Act, 2026) made the 10% BC SR&ED Tax Credit permanent and harmonized provincial rules with federal Bill C-15 by increasing the refundable expenditure limit to $6,000,000, extending refundability to ECPCs, raising the taxable capital phase-out range to $15,000,000–$75,000,000, and restoring capital expenditure eligibility. In Ontario, the 2026 Ontario Economic Outlook and Fiscal Review (Fall Economic Statement), released on October 29, 2026, proposes to restore the eligibility of qualifying capital expenditures on property acquired on or after December 16, 2024 for the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC) and the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC).
1. Executive Summary and the 2024–2026 Legislative Transformation

Canada's SR&ED tax incentive program is a non-discretionary, entitlement-based statutory framework integrated directly into the federal and provincial income tax assessment systems. Unlike competitive grant programs that operate under capped parliamentary appropriations and fixed application windows, any corporation, individual, trust, or partnership carrying on a business in Canada that conducts work meeting the statutory definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act—and that submits the prescribed forms containing the prescribed information on or before the statutory reporting deadline—is legally entitled to claim the resulting income deductions and Investment Tax Credits.
1.1 Chronology of the 2024–2026 Federal SR&ED Reforms

From January 1, 2014, through December 15, 2024, the federal SR&ED program operated under restrictive statutory parameters enacted by the 2012 Federal Budget. During that eleven-year window, expenditures of a capital nature (including Shared-Use Equipment) and equipment lease costs were completely ineligible for SR&ED tax incentives, the basic ITC rate stood at 15% (reduced from 20% prior to 2014), arm's length contract payments and third-party payments were restricted to an 80% inclusion rate for ITC purposes, the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) overhead rate was fixed at 55% of the salary base (reduced from 65% prior to 2013 and 60% in 2013), and the enhanced 35% refundable ITC was limited strictly to Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) on up to $3,000,000 of qualified expenditures, phasing out between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada.

Following national consultations initiated by the Department of Finance Canada in 2024, the federal government announced an initial reform framework in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (FES) in December 2024, which initially proposed raising the enhanced expenditure limit to $4,500,000 and restoring capital expenditures. In Federal Budget 2025, tabled in Parliament on November 4, 2025, the Department of Finance expanded these measures, raising the maximum annual expenditure limit to $6,000,000. The legislative text was introduced in Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1), examined by the House of Commons Standing Committee on Finance in February 2026, and granted Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, with retroactive application to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024.

To implement Bill C-15, the CRA published a sequenced rollout of updated tax forms, schedules, and administrative policies throughout 2026. On April 1, 2026, the CRA launched the new Optional Pre-Claim Approval Process and published updated online calculation pages. On May 15, 2026, the CRA issued the revised Form T661 (Version 26) (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim), Form T1145 (Agreement to Allocate Assistance for SR&ED Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length), and Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length). On May 22, 2026, the CRA published the revised Schedule T2SCH31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations), the updated SR&ED Shared-Use Equipment Policy, the updated Total Qualified SR&ED Expenditures for Investment Tax Credit Purposes Policy, and the updated SR&ED Glossary. On May 29, 2026, the CRA released the updated Schedule T2SCH49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit). In June 2026, the CRA published the updated SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (June 8/22, 2026) and the updated SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (June 29, 2026), followed on October 7, 2026, by the updated SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy.

body.text: 2. Federal Statutory Architecture and the Dual-Pillar Incentive Mechanism

The federal SR&ED program is structured around two distinct statutory mechanisms in the Income Tax Act: Section 37, which governs the computation of net business income through the Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures, and Sections 127 and 127.1, which govern the calculation, application, carryback, carryforward, recapture, and refundability of SR&ED Investment Tax Credits.
2.1 Pillar One: The Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures (ITA Section 37)

Under general income tax rules in paragraph 18(1)(a) and subsection 18(9) of the Income Tax Act, current business outlays are deductible only in the taxation year incurred and capital expenditures must be depreciated over time via Capital Cost Allowance (CCA). Subsection 37(1) overrides these baseline constraints for qualifying SR&ED carried on in Canada by creating a cumulative running account known as the Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures. A taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada in a taxation year may add allowable current and (post-December 15, 2024) capital SR&ED expenditures to this pool and deduct all or any portion of the positive year-end balance in computing net income from the business for tax purposes.

Several foundational statutory rules govern the operation of the Section 37 expenditure pool. First, under subsections 37(1) and 37(1.1), the SR&ED carried on in Canada (including work within Canada's exclusive economic zone under subsection 37(1.3)) must be related to a business of the taxpayer. Where a corporate claimant performs SR&ED related to a business actively carried on by a related corporation—such as a dedicated R&D subsidiary conducting experimental development for a parent or sister corporation at a time when they do not deal at arm's length—subsection 37(1.1) deems the SR&ED to relate to a business of the claimant at that time. Second, under the CRA's Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures Policy, a positive balance in the Section 37 pool does not expire and carries forward indefinitely. The CRA treats the pool as a single running balance without tracking the specific taxation year in which individual expenditures originated. A corporate or individual claimant has full discretion on Line 460 of Form T661 to deduct the entire available pool (Line 455), a partial amount, or zero in a given year, carrying forward any remaining balance on Line 470 to shelter taxable income in future years. Once current-year SR&ED expenditures have been properly identified on Form T661 by the statutory reporting deadline, the subsequent deduction of amounts from the pool in a later taxation year is not subject to the SR&ED reporting deadline.

Third, partnerships are subject to a mandatory deduction rule under paragraph 96(1)(e.1) of the ITA: a partnership cannot carry forward an undeducted balance in the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures to a subsequent fiscal period. Instead, the entire pool balance at the end of the partnership's fiscal period must be deducted in full in computing the partnership's net income or loss for that year, which is then allocated to the partners. Fourth, under paragraph 2902(c) of the Income Tax Regulations, no deduction is allowed under Section 37 for any expenditure made to acquire rights in, or arising out of, SR&ED (such as buying an existing patent or technology licence), ensuring that only the performer or the payer on whose behalf SR&ED was contracted receives the tax incentive. Fifth, under subsection 37(5), if an outlay qualifies as both an SR&ED expenditure under Section 37 and a charitable gift under Section 110.1 (for corporations) or Section 118.1 (for individuals), the taxpayer must deduct the outlay as an SR&ED expenditure and is prohibited from claiming it as a charitable donation. Finally, under subsection 37(2), current expenditures for SR&ED carried on outside Canada (beyond the permissible 10% foreign employee salary cap in subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5)) cannot enter the subsection 37(1) pool and do not earn ITCs, but are deductible as current business expenses in the year incurred.

body.text: Negative Pool Balance (ITA Paragraph 12(1)(v) and Paragraph 12(1)(t)) and Loss Restriction Events (ITA Subsection 37(6.1))

When statutory reductions to the Section 37 pool—most frequently the deduction under paragraph 37(1)(e) for prior-year federal SR&ED ITCs claimed or refunded (which includes ITCs earned on the notional 55% PPA that was never added to the Section 37 pool) or current-year government assistance under paragraph 37(1)(d)—exceed the sum of the opening pool balance and current-year additions, the pool balance turns negative at year-end. Under paragraph 12(1)(v) (and paragraph 12(1)(t)), any negative pool balance must be included directly in the claimant's business income for tax purposes in that taxation year on T2 Schedule 1. In the subsequent taxation year, paragraph 37(1)(c.1) adds the amount included in income under paragraph 12(1)(v) back to the pool, restoring the pool balance to zero.

Furthermore, if a corporation undergoes an acquisition of control (or a trust experiences a new majority-interest beneficiary), a loss restriction event occurs, triggering a deemed taxation year-end immediately before the event. Under paragraph 37(1)(h) and subsection 37(6.1), the undeducted Section 37 pool balance accumulated prior to the loss restriction event is reduced to nil. That pre-acquisition pool balance may only be reinstated and carried forward for deduction in a subsequent taxation year if two cumulative conditions are met: (1) the specific business to which the SR&ED expenditures related is continued by the claimant for profit or with a reasonable expectation of profit throughout that subsequent year; and (2) the deduction is capped at the claimant's net income for that year (before making any Section 37 pool deduction) derived from that same business or a similar business.
3. Technical Eligibility Framework: Subsection 248(1) and CRA Administrative Guidelines

To qualify for SR&ED tax incentives, claimed activities must satisfy the legal definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. As the CRA emphasizes in its eligibility guidelines, what is broadly referred to in industry as "research and development (R&D)" or commercial engineering does not automatically constitute SR&ED for income tax purposes.
3.1 The Statutory Definition in Subsection 248(1) of the ITA

Subsection 248(1) defines "scientific research and experimental development" as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis". Beneath this overarching preamble, the statute divides the definition into three categories of core SR&ED work (paragraphs (a), (b), and (c)), eight exhaustive categories of eligible support work (paragraph (d)), and seven categories of statutorily excluded work (paragraphs (e) through (k)):

Work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to: (1) engineering, (2) design, (3) operations research, (4) mathematical analysis, (5) computer programming, (6) data collection (non-routine), (7) testing (non-routine), or (8) psychological research, where the work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of core work described in paragraph (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer. (Support work is never SR&ED on its own).

Explicitly excludes work with respect to: (e) market research or sales promotion; (f) quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; (g) research in the social sciences or the humanities; (h) prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas; (i) the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, or the commercial use of a new or improved process; (j) style changes; or (k) routine data collection.

body.text: 3.2 Historical Evolution of CRA Administrative Eligibility Guidance
The administrative and judicial interpretation of subsection 248(1) has evolved through four distinct milestones over the past four decades:

items: Pre-1985 IT-439 and the May 1985 Budget Papers: Prior to 1985, Interpretation Bulletin IT-439 governed "applied or basic research" and "development". On May 23, 1985, Finance Minister Michael H. Wilson tabled the Securing Economic Renewal Budget Papers, announcing that the statutory definition would be amended to insert the term "experimental development" specifically to clarify that projects involving only routine engineering or routine product development were excluded.

Information Circular IC 86-4 and IC 86-4R3 (1986–1994): Following a March 4, 1986 clarification from the Department of Finance, Revenue Canada and industry leaders co-developed Information Circular IC 86-4 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development) in 1986, which was reinforced by Department of Finance News Release 92-088 on December 2, 1992, and revised as IC 86-4R3 in 1994. IC 86-4R3 established three foundational criteria for SR&ED: (1) scientific or technological advancement, (2) scientific or technological uncertainty, and (3) scientific and technical content (systematic investigation).

The 1998 Northwest Hydraulic Five-Question Test and the 2012/2015 Policy: In Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839, [1998] 3 CTC 2520 (TCC), Justice Bowman synthesized IC 86-4R3 and subsection 248(1) into Five Questions. On December 19, 2012 (revised April 24, 2015), the CRA replaced IC 86-4R3 with the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy, which evaluated SR&ED in Two Steps: Step 1 determined whether SR&ED existed using the five questions: (1) Was there a scientific or a technological uncertainty? (2) Did the effort involve formulating hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that uncertainty? (3) Was the overall approach adopted consistent with a systematic investigation or search, including formulating and testing the hypotheses by means of experiment or analysis? (4) Was the overall approach undertaken for the purpose of achieving a scientific or a technological advancement? and (5) Was a record of the hypotheses tested and the results kept as the work progressed? Step 2 then determined the extent of eligible support work vs. excluded work.

The August 13, 2021 Modernization — The "Why" and "How" Guidelines: Following a 2020 modernization review, on August 13, 2021, the CRA archived the 2015 policy and published the current Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives. While the underlying statutory text of subsection 248(1) remained unchanged—and the Federal Court of Appeal has confirmed in National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72 that the five-criteria Northwest Hydraulic legal standard remains binding law—the 2021 Guidelines consolidate the five questions into Two Overarching Requirements: the "Why" Requirement (representing Questions 1 and 4) and the "How" Requirement (representing Questions 2, 3, and 5).

body.text: 3.3 Deep Analysis of the "Why" and "How" Requirements

Under the CRA's Guidelines on the eligibility of work for SR&ED tax incentives, an SR&ED project comprises a set of interrelated activities that collectively are necessary to resolve scientific or technological uncertainties in an attempt to achieve specific scientific or technological advancements through a systematic investigation performed by qualified individuals. Every claimed project must satisfy both the "Why" and "How" requirements.
A. The "Why" Requirement (Scientific or Technological Uncertainty and Advancement)

The "Why" requirement evaluates the underlying purpose of the work: it must be conducted for the advancement of scientific knowledge (basic or applied research) or for the purpose of achieving technological advancement (experimental development). In assessing this requirement, the CRA distinguishes between conceptual knowledge (generating or discovering new theories, principles, or predictive models that explain why or how a material, device, product, or process behaves) and factual knowledge (merely gathering measurements, empirical data, or routine parameter observations). Eligible SR&ED must aim to generate conceptual knowledge that remedies an insufficiency in the available scientific or technological knowledge base.

Whether a scientific or technological uncertainty exists is evaluated against the combined baseline of publicly available scientific and technical knowledge worldwide and the internal expertise and resources of the claimant's business environment (taking into account business size, competition, industry sector, and access to technical expertise). When a technical challenge can be overcome by applying standard engineering practices, established methodologies, or publicly available knowledge, no technological uncertainty exists. Conversely, an attempt to resolve genuine scientific or technological uncertainty constitutes an attempt to achieve scientific or technological advancement. Crucially, commercial or technical success is irrelevant to the "Why" requirement: work that fails to achieve its performance objective or is abandoned mid-stream still qualifies as SR&ED if it was undertaken for the purpose of resolving genuine technological uncertainty and generated conceptual knowledge explaining why the hypothesized solution failed.
B. The "How" Requirement (Systematic Investigation or Search)

The "How" requirement governs the execution of the work: it must be carried out as a systematic investigation or search in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. The CRA's 2021 Guidelines break the "How" requirement down into four sequential operational stages:

items: Formulating an Idea or Hypothesis: Starting from an analysis of existing facts and the current state of knowledge, qualified personnel must articulate a specific idea or hypothesis (a proposed causal mechanism, design model, or technological approach) aimed at resolving the identified scientific or technological uncertainty.

Testing the Idea or Hypothesis by Experiment or Analysis: The claimant must systematically test the hypothesis through structured experiments, prototypes, pilot trials, or mathematical/analytical simulations where variables are controlled and outcomes are objectively measured. Unstructured "trial-and-error" tinkering—where parts or code parameters are swapped at random without a governing hypothesis or quantitative measurement—does not satisfy the "How" requirement.

Developing Logical Conclusions: The claimant must analyze the experimental results or findings against the initial hypothesis to formulate logical conclusions, which either resolve the technological uncertainty or inform the modification of the hypothesis for subsequent experimental iterations.

Keeping Contemporaneous Evidence: As an integral component of the "How" requirement, the claimant must preserve documentary evidence generated as the work progresses (such as experimental design protocols, test data and logs, laboratory notebooks, CAD drawings, system architecture diagrams, versioned source code, meeting minutes, internal emails, photographs, videos, and physical scrap records) to substantiate the hypotheses tested and the conclusions reached.

body.text: 3.4 Asset Development, Prototypes, Pilot Plants, and Production Runs

When experimental development overlaps with physical manufacturing or asset construction ("shop-floor SR&ED"), the CRA applies two companion policies: the SR&ED while Developing an Asset Policy (updated July 19, 2016) and the SR&ED During Production Runs Policy (updated July 19, 2016).

Under the SR&ED while Developing an Asset Policy, the CRA classifies physical assets into four categories: (1) prototypes, (2) pilot plants, (3) commercial plants, and (4) custom products or commercial assets. A prototype is an original model built strictly to test a concept or hypothesis that has no commercial application or only nominal residual value once testing is complete; 100% (or ASA) of the labour and materials consumed or transformed in designing, constructing, and testing a prototype qualify as current SR&ED expenditures. Similarly, labour and materials consumed or transformed in resolving the technological uncertainties of developing and operating a pilot plant qualify as SR&ED, whereas work and expenditures normally associated with building a commercial plant (had the technology already existed) are disallowed. When SR&ED occurs during the creation of a custom product or commercial asset intended for sale or internal commercial use, the CRA prohibits the practice of claiming the entire cost of the commercial asset and relying on ITC recapture later. Instead, the claimant must segregate the asset into its constituent components and claim only the specific labour, overhead, contracts, and materials transformed that are directly attributable to resolving the technological uncertainty (along with closely associated components that required redesign due to the SR&ED).

Under the SR&ED During Production Runs Policy, when experimental development is conducted on a commercial manufacturing line, the claimant must establish with contemporaneous evidence whether each specific production run represents Experimental Development with Experimental Production (ED+EP) or Experimental Development with Commercial Production (ED+CP). If the technical considerations and records do not prove that the run was conducted strictly for experimental purposes (ED+EP), the CRA classifies the run as ED+CP, where only the incremental labour, overhead, and input materials exceeding standard commercial production requirements qualify as allowable SR&ED expenditures. In all cases, any excess production (operating the production line beyond the duration or volume strictly required for the SR&ED trial) and all standard commercial production costs are disallowed.
4. Qualifying Expenditures, Overhead Methodologies, and Post-2024 Capital Restoration

Once eligible SR&ED work is delineated, the claimant calculates its Allowable SR&ED Expenditures in Part 3 of Form T661 (which enter the Section 37 deductible pool) and adjusts them in Part 4 of Form T661 to establish Total Qualified SR&ED Expenditures (which earn ITCs under Section 127).
4.1 The Annual Election: Proxy Method vs. Traditional Method

Under subsection 37(10) of the Income Tax Act and the CRA's Traditional and Proxy Methods Policy, a claimant must elect on Form T661 for each taxation year whether to compute its SR&ED expenditures using the Proxy Method (Line 160) or the Traditional Method (Line 162). This election applies across all projects for that taxation year and is irrevocable once Form T661 is filed for the year (if no election is made on the initial filing for the year, the Traditional Method applies by default).

Under the Proxy Method, the claimant does not specifically identify, track, or allocate actual SR&ED overhead and other expenditures on Form T661. Instead, actual overhead expenses (such as office supplies, utilities, clerical support salaries, employer payroll benefits, travel, training, and cloud/software subscriptions) remain deductible as ordinary business expenses under paragraph 18(1)(a) of the ITA, while the claimant calculates a notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) equal to 55% of the SR&ED salary base under subsection 2900(4) of the Income Tax Regulations. The PPA is entered on Line 502 of Form T661 and earns federal (and applicable provincial) ITCs, though it is never added to the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool. Conversely, under the Traditional Method, the claimant foregoes the PPA and instead tracks, substantiates, and claims actual overhead and other expenditures that are directly related and incremental to the prosecution of SR&ED on Line 360 of Form T661, which both enter the Section 37 deductible pool and earn ITCs.

4.2 Detailed Rules for Salaries and Wages (CRA SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy)

Under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act and the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy (updated January 28, 2025), "salary or wages" means income of a taxpayer from an office or employment as computed under subdivision a of Division B of Part I of the Act (including sections 5 and 6, and generally corresponding to gross employment wages reported on T4 slips). Allowable salary or wages include regular base pay, vacation pay, statutory holiday pay, sick leave pay, pay in lieu of termination notice, tips/gratuities, honorariums, director's and management fees, commissions, inducement or non-competition payments, section 6 taxable benefits (where cash outlays are made or where non-cash benefits reasonably reflect actual cost excluding GST/HST/PST and are not double-claimed as business expenses), and—for non-specified employees only—enforceable bonuses and remuneration based on profits.

Conversely, SR&ED salary or wages strictly exclude: (1) the employer's share of related payroll benefits (such as employer CPP, EI, provincial health tax, workers' compensation, or pension contributions, though these may be claimed as overhead on Line 360 under the Traditional Method); (2) extended vacation or extended sick leave (during which the employee is not directly engaged in SR&ED); (3) stock option benefits (or shares issued on or after November 17, 2005, where no actual cash outlay is incurred by the corporation); (4) retiring allowances (which may only be considered as overhead under the Traditional Method); and (5) superannuation or pension benefits.
Directly Engaged Employees vs. Specified Employees and the YMPE Caps

Only the portion of an employee's time spent on hands-on SR&ED tasks ("directly engaged in SR&ED")—including hands-on experimentation, direct first-line technical supervision, and short-term technological planning for ongoing SR&ED projects—is claimed on Lines 300 to 309 of Form T661 (unless the employee spends 90% or more [ASA] of their time on SR&ED, in which case 100% of their eligible salary qualifies).

Special statutory caps apply to any "specified employee", defined in subsection 248(1) of the ITA as an employee who does not deal at arm's length with the employer or who is a "specified shareholder" owning, directly or indirectly at any time in the year (together with non-arm's length relatives such as a spouse, sibling, or parent), 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or a related corporation. Specified employees are governed by three cumulative restrictions:

items: Zero Bonuses or Profit-Based Remuneration (ITA Clauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) and (B)): Bonuses and remuneration based on profits paid to a specified employee are completely disallowed for SR&ED purposes.

Allowable Expenditure Ceiling — 5 × YMPE (ITA Subsection 37(9.1)): For the Section 37 deductible pool and base allowable salary on Line 305 of Form T661, the maximum SR&ED salary or wages claimable for a specified employee in a taxation year is capped at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year that the individual is a specified employee (5 × YMPE × [Days as Specified Employee ÷ 365]). If a specified employee performs SR&ED for multiple associated corporations, this 5 × YMPE ceiling must be allocated across the associated group by filing Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for SR&ED) together with a certified copy of the directors' resolution authorizing the agreement.

Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Salary Base Ceiling — Lesser of 75% of Total Salary or 2.5 × YMPE (ITR Subsections 2900(7), 2900(8), and 2900(9)): In Part 5 of Form T661 (Lines 810 to 820), the salary base for the 55% PPA first excludes all bonuses, profit-based remuneration, section 6 taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages paid in the year (Line 310) for all employees under ITR Subsection 2900(9). Then, for each specified employee listed in Table 7 (Boxes 850–860), ITR Subsection 2900(7) limits the salary base inclusion in Box 860 (Line 816) to the lesser of: (a) Box 856, which multiplies the specified employee's total eligible salary for the year (SR&ED and non-SR&ED combined, excluding bonuses, profit pay, taxable benefits, and prior unpaid wages in Box 852) by the percentage of time spent directly engaged in SR&ED in Box 854, capped at a maximum of 75%; or (b) Box 858, equal to 2.5 times the YMPE for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year that the individual was employed by the claimant (2.5 × YMPE × [Days Employed ÷ 365], shared across associated corporations under ITR Subsection 2900(8)).

body.text: Permissible Foreign Salary or Wages (ITA Subsections 37(1.4) & 37(1.5)) and the 180-Day Unpaid Rules (ITA Subsections 78(4) & 127(26))

Under subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5) of the ITA, a claimant may claim "permissible salary or wages" paid to its own employees for SR&ED work carried on outside Canada (Form T661, Lines 265, 307, and 309) if four conditions are met: (1) the work is directly undertaken by the taxpayer's employees (never foreign contractors); (2) the work relates to a business of the taxpayer; (3) the work is performed solely in support of SR&ED carried on in Canada by the taxpayer; and (4) the salary or wages are not subject to an income or profits tax from another country. Under subsection 37(1.5), permissible foreign wages are capped at 10% of the total directly engaged Canadian SR&ED salaries and wages claimed on Lines 300 and 305.

Two statutory 180-day unpaid amount rules also govern expenditure timing. First, under subsection 78(4) of the ITA, any salary or wages accrued in a taxation year that remain unpaid 180 days after the end of the taxation year are deemed not to have been incurred in that year, and are instead deemed incurred in the subsequent year when actually paid (reported as unpaid on Line 315 in the year accrued and claimed on Line 310 in the year paid, though excluded from the PPA salary base under ITR s. 2900(9)). Second, under subsection 127(26) of the ITA, current SR&ED expenditures other than salary or wages (such as arm's length contracts, materials, or overhead) unpaid 180 days after year-end are excluded from Qualified SR&ED Expenditures on Line 520 of Form T661 and only earn an ITC in the subsequent year when paid (added on Line 500)—provided they were properly identified on Form T661 within the original 18-month reporting deadline for the year incurred. For an unpaid arm's length SR&ED contract, the expenditure is first reduced by 20% to 80%, that 80% is deducted on Line 520, and when subsequently paid, 80% of the paid amount is added back on Line 500.
4.3 Traditional Method Overhead Rules and the Overall Cap on the PPA (ITR Subsection 2900(6))

When a claimant elects the Traditional Method, paragraph 2900(2)(c) and subsection 2900(3) of the Income Tax Regulations and the CRA's SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy (updated October 14, 2022) require every claimed overhead expenditure (or allocated portion thereof) on Line 360 to satisfy two mandatory tests:

items: The "Directly Related" Test: The expenditure must link directly—without any intervening step or intermediary—to the SR&ED work itself, the SR&ED staff, or the machinery/equipment used by staff to perform SR&ED. Expenditures incurred after an SR&ED project has finished (such as post-project scrap or waste disposal) generally fail this test, with a narrow exception for qualifying retiring allowances.

The "Incremental" Test: The expenditure would not have been incurred had the prosecution of SR&ED not occurred. Applying a flat headcount percentage to general corporate expenses (such as claiming 25% of total company travel or fixed monthly telephone/internet plans because 25% of employees perform SR&ED) is disallowed. However, utilities (electricity, natural gas, water) that vary directly with the operating time of SR&ED equipment, incremental cloud computing environments dedicated to R&D model training/testing (segregated from live production COGS), direct clerical/administrative staff supporting SR&ED personnel, employer payroll benefits on SR&ED wages, recruitment/relocation costs for SR&ED staff, clinical trial volunteer fees, and Canadian travel/training directly for SR&ED trials qualify. Conversely, third-party fees paid to consultants or accountants to prepare the SR&ED claim itself, convention/conference fees, legal/accounting fees, entertainment, advertising, and interest/financing costs under paragraphs 20(1)(c)–(g) are prescribed expenditures under ITR Section 2902 and cannot earn an ITC (though internal employee salaries for preparing an SR&ED claim are not prescribed expenditures if directly related and incremental).

body.text: When a claimant instead elects the Proxy Method, the PPA calculated at 55% of the salary base on Line 820 is subject to the Overall Cap on the Prescribed Proxy Amount under subsection 2900(6) of the Income Tax Regulations. Under the CRA's Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy, the Overall Cap is calculated as A − B − C, where A is the total of all amounts deducted in computing net income for tax purposes from the business for the year (including Cost of Goods Sold); B is the total of specific statutory deductions identified in the Regulations, such as Capital Cost Allowance (CCA), the Section 37 SR&ED pool deduction claimed on Line 411 of Schedule T2SCH1, and interest expenses; and C is the total of building rent/use deductions. The claimant enters the lesser of Line 820 and the Regulation 2900(6) Overall Cap onto Line 502 of Form T661.
4.4 Materials Consumed and Materials Transformed (CRA Materials for SR&ED Policy)

Under ITA Subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I)/(II) and (B)(V), ITR Paragraph 2900(2)(a), and the CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy, claimants under both the Traditional and Proxy methods may claim the laid-down cost (invoice cost, customs/excise duties, transportation, and storage, or direct labour and overhead for self-manufactured inventory, excluding internal profit for non-arm's length purchases under s. 127(11.6)) of materials consumed (Line 320) or materials transformed (Line 325) in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada, strictly in the taxation year in which the material is actually consumed or transformed.

To constitute "materials for SR&ED," the items must be physical, tangible substances or components (in a solid, liquid, or gaseous state) that at a given moment in the SR&ED process compose the body of a tangible object ("thing") on which SR&ED is performed or that results from the SR&ED. Materials consumed are rendered virtually valueless (less than 10% of original cost) or destroyed as a direct result of the SR&ED (including galvanization or third-party processing costs applied to a test part prior to destructive SR&ED testing, as well as seeds, agar, fungal media, and field-plot fertilizers/pesticides in agricultural SR&ED). Materials transformed retain value after being physically incorporated into a prototype, pilot plant, custom asset, or experimental production, and remain subject to ITC Recapture under subsections 127(27) to (36) if subsequently sold or converted to commercial use. Laboratory supplies (petri dishes, beakers, flasks, pipettes), cleaning supplies, lubricants, CDs/DVDs, and utilities (electricity, gas, water) do not compose the body of the object of SR&ED and cannot be claimed as materials.

4.6 Post-December 15, 2024 Restoration of Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and Lease Costs

Enacted on March 26, 2026 through Bill C-15, capital property and equipment lease expenditures incurred after December 15, 2024 are once again eligible for federal SR&ED deductions and ITCs under three specific regimes:

items: SR&ED Capital Expenditures — The ≥90% ASA Intent Test (ITA Paragraph 37(1)(b); Form T661 Line 390): Under the updated SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (June 29, 2026), an outlay to acquire depreciable property (under subsection 13(21)) that is acquired and becomes available for use (under subsection 37(1.2)) after December 15, 2024, qualifies on Line 390 of Form T661 if, at the time of acquisition, the claimant intended either that (a) the property would be used during all or substantially all (90% or more) of its operating time in its expected useful life for SR&ED in Canada, or (b) 90% or more (ASA) of its value would be consumed in SR&ED in Canada. Land, buildings, and leasehold interests in buildings are excluded under paragraph 37(8)(d), and General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF) is excluded if the Proxy Method is elected (though eligible under the Traditional Method). While both new and used ASA depreciable property enter the Section 37 deductible pool on Line 390 (and must not be claimed for regular CCA on Schedule T2SCH8), used equipment is deducted on Line 532 of Form T661 and does not earn an ITC unless refurbished by the vendor prior to sale to a state equivalent to new equipment. Claimants must report the 10 most expensive post-December 15, 2024 capital properties per project on Lines 262 and 263 of Part 2 and the 20 most expensive properties overall in Part 6B (Boxes 780, 782, and 786).

Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) — The >50% to <90% Actual Use Test (ITA Subsection 127(9); Form T661 Line 504): Under the updated SR&ED Shared-Use Equipment Policy (May 22, 2026), new depreciable machinery and equipment acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024 that does not meet the 90% ASA test—and is neither GPOEF nor Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) under ITR Subsection 2900(11) (which excludes property intended at acquisition to be used for SR&ED during the assembly, construction, or commissioning of a commercial manufacturing plant/line [para 2900(11)(c)] or intended at acquisition to be used primarily for non-SR&ED over its expected useful life [para 2900(11)(d)])—earns SR&ED ITCs on Line 504 of Form T661 (and Box 794 of Part 6B) based on actual primary use (more than 50% but less than 90% of operating time). For First-Term SUE (evaluated from acquisition to the end of the first taxation year ending at least 12 months later), 25% (1/4) of the capital cost (excluding borrowed money costs under section 21 and adjusted for non-arm's length costs under subsection 127(11.6)) qualifies on Line 504. For Second-Term SUE (evaluated from acquisition to the end of the first taxation year ending at least 24 months later, provided it qualified as First-Term SUE), an additional 25% (1/4) of the capital cost qualifies on Line 504. SUE capital cost does not enter the Section 37 pool and is instead depreciated via regular CCA on Schedule T2SCH8.

Equipment Lease Expenditures (Post-December 15, 2024 — Form T661 Lines 350, 355, 360 & Box 759): Under the updated SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (June 2026), equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024 qualify based on the method elected. Under the Traditional Method, leased equipment (including GPOEF) used ≥90% (ASA) of its operating time in the tax year for SR&ED in Canada is 100% claimable on Line 350, while leased equipment (and leased land) used <90% for SR&ED is claimable on Line 360 as overhead proportional to its SR&ED operating time if directly related and incremental. Under the Proxy Method (which excludes GPOEF and land leases), leased equipment used ≥90% (ASA) for SR&ED is 100% claimable on Line 350 (ITA Subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I)), leased equipment used primarily (>50% to <90%) for SR&ED is 50% claimable on Line 355 (ITA Subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(VI)), and equipment used ≤50% for SR&ED is ineligible. Building lease/rent payments remain strictly disallowed under paragraphs 37(8)(d) and (e) unless the building is a prescribed special-purpose building approved by the Department of Finance.

body.text: 5.2 Expenditure Limit Calculations and Phase-Out Mechanics (ITA Subsections 127(10.2) to 127(10.64))

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the maximum annual Expenditure Limit eligible for the enhanced 35% ITC rate (15% basic + 20% enhancement under subsection 127(10.1)) is $6,000,000 (doubled from $3,000,000 for taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024). Qualified expenditures exceeding the corporation's expenditure limit earn the basic 15% ITC rate.

For a Canadian-Controlled Private Corporation (CCPC) (defined in subsection 125(7)), the $6,000,000 expenditure limit under subsections 127(10.2) and 127(10.21) begins to phase out linearly when the prior taxation year's taxable capital employed in Canada (determined under section 181.2 or 181.3 for the CCPC and all associated corporations) reaches $15,000,000, and is completely eliminated ($0) at $75,000,000. Specifically, the post-December 15, 2024 CCPC expenditure limit is calculated as $6,000,000 × [($60,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000], where A is nil if prior-year taxable capital is $15,000,000 or less, or the lesser of $60,000,000 and the excess of prior-year taxable capital over $15,000,000 (reducing the $6,000,000 limit by $1.00 for every $10.00 of taxable capital above $15,000,000). Associated CCPCs must allocate the group expenditure limit among themselves by filing Schedule T2SCH49 under subsection 127(10.3).

For an Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC)—defined in subsection 127(9) as a public corporation resident in Canada (or a ≥90%-owned eligible subsidiary) that is not controlled directly or indirectly by non-residents and would not be controlled by a single person if all non-resident-owned shares were held by one person—the $6,000,000 expenditure limit under subsections 127(10.6), 127(10.61), and 127(10.62) phases out using the Revenue Method based on the average annual revenue reflected in the financial statements of the ECPC (and its consolidated group) over the preceding 3 fiscal years. The ECPC expenditure limit begins to decrease once 3-year average annual revenue exceeds $15,000,000 and becomes nil ($0) at $75,000,000. Under subsections 127(10.31) and 127(10.32), a single CCPC or an associated group of CCPCs may also elect on the prescribed form to compute its $6,000,000 expenditure limit using the 3-year average annual revenue method ($15,000,000–$75,000,000) instead of the taxable capital method. Short taxation years prorate the expenditure limit by the number of days in the taxation year divided by 365 under subsection 127(10.5).
5.3 Carryback, Carryforward, Loss Restrictions, and Recapture of ITCs

Unused SR&ED ITCs remaining after offsetting current-year Part I tax under subsection 127(5) and claiming any cash refund under section 127.1 (which is deemed to be a deduction against Part I tax under subsection 127.1(3)) may be carried back up to 3 preceding taxation years (limited to the lesser of the current-year unused non-deductible ITC and the net Part I tax payable in that prior year) or carried forward up to 20 subsequent taxation years. Note that ITCs generated by repayments of government assistance or contract payments under subsections 127(10.7) and 127(10.8) are non-refundable and are calculated at the historical ITC rate that applied when the assistance originally reduced the expenditure pool. Upon an acquisition of control (loss restriction event), subsections 127(9.1) and 127(9.2) restrict the carryforward of pre-acquisition ITCs and the carryback of post-acquisition ITCs to Part I tax payable from carrying on that same or a similar business.

Under subsections 127(27) to 127(36) of the ITA and the CRA's Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, if a taxpayer disposes of a property on which it earned an SR&ED ITC (including materials transformed into a prototype, custom asset, or experimental production, post-December 15, 2024 ASA capital property, or Shared-Use Equipment) or converts it to commercial use within 20 preceding taxation years, the taxpayer must add a recapture amount to its Part I tax payable on Schedule T2SCH31. The recapture equals the lesser of: (1) the actual SR&ED ITC earned on the property, and (2) the historical ITC percentage applied to the proceeds of disposition (in an arm's length sale) or the fair market value (FMV) (upon conversion to commercial use or non-arm's length transfer)—using 25% of the proceeds/FMV for First-Term SUE and 50% for Second-Term SUE. Crucially, under subsection 127(32), the "cost" of property for recapture is limited to amounts paid to acquire tangible property from a third party and never includes internal in-house salaries, wages, or overhead incurred to manufacture or transform the prototype, nor does recapture ever apply to the sale or licensing of intellectual property (IP) accrued to the payer. Any recaptured ITC added to Part I tax increases the Section 37 deductible pool in the following taxation year under paragraph 37(1)(c.2).
6. Government Assistance, Contract Payments, and Grant Stacking Mechanics

Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsections 127(18), 127(19), and 127(20) of the Income Tax Act, along with the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy, a claimant must reduce both its Section 37 Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures and its Section 127 Qualified SR&ED Expenditures by any government assistance, non-government assistance, or contract payment in respect of SR&ED that the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before the filing due date of its income tax return for the taxation year (Form T661, Lines 513 to 517).
6.1 Statutory Scope of Assistance and Project-by-Project Grind Rules

Government assistance is defined in subsection 127(9) as assistance from a government, municipality, or other public authority (including Crown corporations, foreign governments, and government-funded non-profit intermediaries) in the form of a grant, subsidy, forgivable loan (including conditionally repayable loans where repayment depends on project revenues or expires after a set term), deduction from tax, investment allowance, or any other form of assistance other than the federal SR&ED ITC. This encompasses direct R&D contributions such as the National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP) and Global Innovation Clusters contributions, as well as provincial and territorial R&D tax credits. Non-government assistance covers inducements, reimbursements, or contributions included under paragraph 12(1)(x), while contract payments cover amounts payable by an arm's length taxable supplier, government, or tax-exempt entity for SR&ED performed on its behalf.

Under CRA policy, assistance reduces SR&ED expenditures strictly on a project-by-project basis. If assistance received for Project 1 exceeds Project 1's SR&ED expenditures, Project 1's qualified expenditures are reduced to nil ($0), and the excess assistance cannot reduce the expenditures of Project 2; instead, the excess is included in income under paragraph 12(1)(x) (or allocated to a non-arm's length group member performing the same project via Form T1145 under subsection 127(20)).

body.text: 7.2 Deep Dive: Québec's CRIC Regime, British Columbia's Bill 2 (2026), and Ontario's Three-Credit Suite

In Québec, the Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) applies to taxation years (or partnership fiscal periods) beginning after March 25, 2025, replacing eight former Québec R&D credits. While Québec's R&D definition is harmonized with federal subsection 248(1) (and reviewed scientifically by the CRA), CRIC uniquely expands eligibility to pre-commercialization activities carried out in Québec in conjunction with Québec R&D—specifically: (1) tests, technological validations, and studies required to obtain an initial regulatory approval or certification to commercialize an innovation (including implementing a quality control system strictly required for initial certification), and (2) product design, including the development of form, shape, aesthetics, improved functionality, and choice of materials. Qualified CRIC expenditures include 100% of Québec employee salaries, 50% of payments to Québec subcontractors, 50% of payments to eligible Québec public research centres, research consortia, or university entities, and 100% of acquisition costs for new depreciable capital property (excluding land and buildings) used almost exclusively (≥90%) in Québec for eligible activities. Claimants must subtract an Applicable Exclusion Threshold equal to the greater of $50,000 (prorated for short years) or the sum of employee basic personal amount thresholds adjusted for time spent on eligible activities. Net qualified expenditures above the threshold earn a 30% refundable credit on the first $1,000,000 (shared among associated corporations via Form RD-1029.8.EN-T; corporate partners of a partnership earn 20% only) and 20% refundable on the excess, claimed on Form RD-1029.8.CR-T (and Form RD-1029.8.PR-T for pre-commercialization). If capital property claimed under CRIC ceases to be used solely in Québec within 730 consecutive days, the credit is recovered via a special tax.

In British Columbia, Part 6 (Sections 97 to 103) of the Income Tax Act (B.C.) and Bill 2 (Budget Measures Implementation Act, 2026) permanently removed the statutory sunset date for the BC SR&ED Tax Credit and aligned it with federal Bill C-15 for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024. Both CCPCs and Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) with a BC permanent establishment can claim a 10% fully refundable credit on up to $6,000,000 of SR&ED qualified BC expenditures (up to $600,000 refundable annually, phasing out over $15,000,000–$75,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital or federal ECPC revenue), while non-CCPC/ECPC corporations, active corporate partners of partnerships (under section 99.1), and expenditures above the $6,000,000 limit earn a 10% non-refundable credit (carryback 3 years, carryforward 10 years). Capital expenditures acquired after December 15, 2024 are fully restored to the BC credit base, subject to a 10-year BC recapture rule under section 102.1 (25% of proceeds/FMV for First-Term SUE, 50% for Second-Term SUE, 100% for other property). Note that under BC law, a corporation cannot claim both the BC Interactive Digital Media Tax Credit (IDMTC) and the BC SR&ED Tax Credit in the same taxation year.

In Ontario, corporations can stack up to three complementary credits: (1) the 8% refundable OITC (Schedule 566) on up to $3,000,000 of Ontario qualified expenditures (capital expenditures made after December 31, 2013 are currently excluded, although the 2026 Fall Economic Statement proposes to restore qualifying capital expenditures on property acquired on or after December 16, 2024 for both the OITC and the ORDTC; phasing out between $500,000–$800,000 of prior-year federal taxable income and $25,000,000–$50,000,000 of taxable capital); (2) the 3.5% non-refundable ORDTC (Schedule 508) on all eligible Ontario expenditures without a cap; and (3) the 20% refundable OBRITC (Schedules 568 and 569) on up to $20,000,000 annually of current money payments under eligible contracts with Ontario universities, community colleges, hospital research institutes, or Ontario Centres of Excellence (provided the corporation is not "connected" to the research institute through >10% voting shares or >10% fair market value equity). Where a corporation in a tax loss position earns a non-refundable provincial credit (such as the 3.5% Ontario ORDTC, 10% non-refundable BC credit, or 10% non-refundable Saskatchewan credit), it may waive or renounce that credit by its filing due date (6 months after year-end) so the uncollectible credit does not grind its 35% refundable federal SR&ED ITC under ITA paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(18).

body.text: 8.3 The New Optional Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026 — Form T1322)

Launched on April 1, 2026, the CRA's Optional Pre-Claim Approval Process enables businesses to have their planned R&D projects evaluated for technical SR&ED eligibility before beginning the work or incurring significant costs. To qualify for pre-claim approval, the business must be a CCPC, another Canadian corporation, or a Canadian partnership, have gross business income of less than $25,000,000, and be in good standing with the CRA; the project(s) (up to a maximum of 3 projects per application) must not have been included in a prior SR&ED claim and must not involve issues currently under litigation.
The application and evaluation process follows four sequential steps:

items: Request a Pre-Claim Approval Case Number: The claimant submits an online request web form on Canada.ca (which takes under five minutes). The CRA verifies threshold eligibility and provides a Case Number within 2 business days via My Business Account for existing SR&ED claimants in good standing, or within 5 business days by telephone for all other businesses.

Complete and Submit Form T1322 in My Business Account: Using the assigned Case Number, the claimant completes Form T1322 (Application for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) pre-claim approval)—providing business identification (Lines 010–016), project title, anticipated start date, and estimated total SR&ED expenditures (Lines 020–024), lead technical contact, concise Section B technical responses (existing state of knowledge, scientific/technological uncertainty, initial hypothesis, and planned experiments/analyses), preparer disclosure (Lines 050–060), and authorized signing officer certification (Lines 080–082)—and uploads Form T1322 along with internal project planning documentation via My Business Account.

Attend the Technical Review Meeting with an RTA (Within 4 Weeks): The CRA assigns a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA). Within 4 weeks of submitting Form T1322, the RTA conducts a virtual or on-site meeting (estimated duration 2 to 5 hours) with the business's technical personnel to discuss the state of technology, uncertainty, and planned investigation. This meeting is mandatory for new SR&ED claimants and at the RTA's discretion for existing claimants in good standing.

Receive Formal Determination (Within 8 Weeks): Within 8 weeks of submitting the completed application in My Business Account, the CRA issues a formal Pre-Claim Approval Evaluation Report confirming whether pre-claim approval is granted (along with detailed rationale and recommendations). Once granted, pre-claim approval is valid for up to 3 years, and when the claimant later files Form T661 (reporting the case number on Lines 212 and 214), any post-filing expenditure review for pre-approved projects is processed under an accelerated 90-calendar-day service standard instead of 180 days.

body.text: 9. CRA Audit Protocols, Compliance Penalties, and Dispute Resolution
9.1 CRA Processing Timeframes, Service Standards, and Review Execution

For refundable SR&ED claims, the CRA maintains three distinct processing service standards (measured from the date the CRA receives both the complete SR&ED claim and the income tax return for the year; non-refundable claims do not have a published service standard): (1) within 60 calendar days for refundable claims accepted as filed without review; (2) within 90 calendar days for refundable claims selected for an expenditure-only review where all claimed projects were granted Pre-Claim Approval (and did not materially change); and (3) within 180 calendar days (targeted 90% of the time) for refundable claims selected for review that include any project not granted pre-claim approval or that materially differs from a pre-approved project. First-time claimants (or claimants who have not filed in the preceding 3 years) may also be selected for the mandatory First-Time Claimant Advisory Service (FTCAS).

Under The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants (updated July 2, 2025), a full review is conducted collaboratively by a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) (who evaluates technical eligibility under subsection 248(1) and prepares the SR&ED Project Eligibility Report, reporting to a Research and Technology Manager [RTM]) and a Financial Reviewer (FR) (who audits expenditure allowability, T4 payroll, contracts, assistance, and ITC calculations, reporting to a Financial Review Manager [FRM]). The review proceeds through three steps: (1) Step 1 (Start of Review), involving an initial telephone contact, issue identification, and an initial letter with a meeting agenda and pre-meeting information requests (typically allowing a 30-day response window); (2) Step 2 (Review Meeting & Information Requests), featuring interviews with technical and financial personnel, a virtual or on-site tour of the premises, inspection of contemporaneous evidence matching Lines 270–282 of Form T661, and sharing of preliminary findings (if documentation is deficient, reviewers may issue a formal "Better Books and Records" letter requiring a signed compliance agreement within 30 days); and (3) Step 3 (End of Review), where the RTA and FR issue a Proposal Package (comprising the SR&ED Project Eligibility Report, financial adjustment schedule, and Proposal Letter), giving the claimant 30 calendar days to submit written representations before a Notice of Assessment or Reassessment is issued.
9.2 Gross Negligence Penalties on Overstated SR&ED Claims

Under the CRA's Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims Policy (updated January 28, 2025), a claimant that knowingly or under circumstances amounting to gross negligence files an overstated SR&ED claim is subject to gross negligence penalties on the resulting understatement of Part I tax payable and/or overstatement of refundable ITCs claimed. Under CRA ordering rules, the claimant is deemed to have deducted its overstated Section 37 pool or overstated ITC before any valid opening, transferred, or current-year credits. For example, in the policy's comparative audit tables, where a CCPC earning the 35% enhanced ITC rate files $400,000 of SR&ED salaries and $240,000 of materials ($640,000 allowable pool + $220,000 PPA at 55% = $860,000 qualified expenditures; $301,000 ITC claimed), and the CRA audit revises eligible salaries to $200,000 and materials to $220,000 ($420,000 allowable pool + $110,000 PPA = $530,000 qualified expenditures; $185,500 ITC allowed), the gross negligence penalty base is computed on the $220,000 pool overstatement and the $115,500 overstated ITC ($330,000 qualified expenditure difference × 35%). As the CRA explicitly warns, the signing officer and claimant remain legally responsible for the accuracy of the claim even if misled by third-party promotional consultants.
9.3 Five-Tier Escalation Ladder for Resolving SR&ED Disputes
Under the CRA's Guidelines for resolving claimants' SR&ED concerns (updated December 5, 2025), claimants have access to a structured five-tier dispute resolution framework:

items: Step 1 — Direct Discussion with the RTA and/or FR: Raise factual or technical clarifications directly with the assigned reviewers as soon as concerns arise during the review.

Step 2 — Escalation to the Research and Technology Manager (RTM) and/or Financial Review Manager (FRM): Request the involvement of the RTM and/or FRM to review the facts of the case and the positions of both the claimant and the reviewer.

Step 3 — Request an Administrative Review via Form RC532: After receiving the Proposal Package—and strictly before the expiry of the 30-day proposal period and before the review file is closed—the claimant may notify the reviewers and mail Form RC532 (Request for an Administrative Review) to the National SR&ED Administrative Review Intake Centre (Canada Revenue Agency, Business Tax Incentives Directorate, Enterprise Building, 13th Floor, 427 Laurier Ave W, Ottawa ON K1A 0L5). Within 3 business days, the Intake Centre forwards the request to the local SR&ED Assistant Director, who evaluates whether (a) the claimant was accorded due process and (b) the technical and financial reviews complied with current SR&ED legislation, policies, and procedures, issuing a written determination of either Decision Maintained or Decision Reconsidered.

Step 4 — Formal Notice of Objection to the CRA Appeals Branch: Within 90 calendar days from the date of the Notice of Assessment or Reassessment, the claimant may file a formal Notice of Objection to initiate an independent review by the CRA Appeals Branch.

Step 5 — Judicial Appeal to the Tax Court of Canada and Federal Court of Appeal (ITA Section 169): If the claimant disagrees with the CRA Appeals Branch's decision on the objection, the claimant may file a Notice of Appeal with the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) under the Income Tax Act (with further appellate review before the Federal Court of Appeal [FCA]).

body.text: 10. Landmark Canadian Jurisprudence and Judicial Precedents

Canadian courts have established a rigorous body of case law interpreting subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act and former Regulation 2900. The following landmark decisions govern technical eligibility, scientific methodology, expert witness admissibility, and contemporaneous documentation across all SR&ED audits and appeals:
10.1 Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839, [1998] 3 CTC 2520, 1998 CanLII 553 (TCC)

In Northwest Hydraulic, the appellant engineering consulting firm claimed SR&ED tax incentives for physical scale-model hydraulic and river engineering projects, which the Minister denied as routine civil engineering. Ruling in favour of the taxpayer, Justice Bowman articulated at paragraph 16 the foundational Five-Question Legal Test for SR&ED: (1) Is there a technical risk or uncertainty that cannot be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures? (where "routine engineering" describes techniques, procedures, and data generally accessible to competent professionals in the field); (2) Did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty? (requiring a five-stage process: observation of the subject matter of the problem, formulation of a clear objective, identification and articulation of the technological uncertainty, formulation of a hypothesis or hypotheses designed to reduce or eliminate the uncertainty, and methodical and systematic testing of the hypotheses); (3) Did the procedures adopted accord with established and objective principles of the scientific method, characterized by trained and systematic observation, measurement and experiment, and the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses?; (4) Did the process result in a technological advance, that is to say an advancement in the general understanding?; and (5) Did the taxpayer keep a detailed record of the hypotheses, tests, and results as the work progressed?.
10.2 RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, 99 DTC 5087, [1999] 1 CTC 132 (FCA) and C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2001 FCA 393, 2002 DTC 6740 (FCA)

In RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, 99 DTC 5087 (FCA), the Federal Court of Appeal formally adopted Justice Bowman's five Northwest Hydraulic criteria at the appellate level and held that repeatability is an essential attribute of true scientific research and experimental development. Because scientific experimentation must be verifiable and repeatable, the Court ruled that a claimant must produce contemporaneous documentary evidence of the tests conducted and the experimental results obtained as the work progressed, rather than relying solely on after-the-fact oral testimony.

Three years later, in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2001 FCA 393, the appellant sought SR&ED credits for the 1991–1995 development of a large-scale multilingual telemarketing and computer database software system (IDLS) handling 2 to 3 million lottery customers and up to 25,000 daily purchases. Dismissing the appeal from the bench (per Sexton J.A.), the Federal Court of Appeal codified the five-part Northwest Hydraulic / RIS-Christie test at paragraph 17 and affirmed the Tax Court's reliance on Crown expert testimony showing that even highly complex custom software development does not constitute SR&ED when the technical challenges can be resolved by routine software engineering or standard programming procedures.
10.3 Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 6 (TCC)

In Joel Theatrical Rigging, the appellant claimed SR&ED in its 2008 and 2009 taxation years for two mechanical/hydraulic rigging projects: the Fire Curtain Project (controlling the descent rate of a theatre fire curtain within 30 seconds using a motorized hydraulic backwind system without counterweights) and the Manual Override Project (developing a manual hand-crank override for a motorized stage curtain that preserved automated limit-switch calibration). Justice Sommerfeldt dismissed both appeals, holding that: (1) without expert engineering testimony establishing the state of the art, the taxpayer failed to prove that the problems exceeded routine engineering; (2) rearranging hydraulic valves, pumps, and sprockets until a setup worked was ad hoc trial-and-error, not the formulation and testing of scientific hypotheses; (3) "guesstimating" test weights at 800–1,000 lbs and judging curtain descent speed solely with the naked eye without recorded measurements failed the scientific method; (4) creating a commercially novel product does not automatically establish a technological advancement in general engineering knowledge; and (5) discarding failed working sketches and relying on retroactive "Experiment Summary Sheets" drafted after the fact by an external SR&ED tax consultant failed the contemporaneous documentation requirement.
10.4 National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72 (aff'g 2020 TCC 47) and Recent TCC Jurisprudence (2021–2025)

In National R&D Inc. v. The Queen, 2020 TCC 47, aff'd National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72, an SR&ED and IT consulting firm claimed SR&ED for developing a web-based Project Tracking System ("PTS Project") constrained to a legacy multi-tiered software architecture (Classic ASP, ADO, COM+, and Microsoft SQL Server 2000). In the Tax Court, Justice Lafleur held that Criterion 1 (technological uncertainty) was satisfied because a claimant's existing architectural and business constraints are relevant context in assessing whether a solution was predictable via routine engineering within that framework (though in 6398316 Canada Inc. v. The Queen, 2021 TCC 17, Justice Lafleur clarified that pure economic or cost-efficiency obstacles alone cannot create technological uncertainty). However, the Tax Court dismissed National R&D's appeal under Criteria 2, 3, 4, and 5 because isolated snippets of early and final source code and employee time-tracking logs failed to demonstrate how hypotheses were systematically tested and modified under the scientific method. Affirming the dismissal in 2022 FCA 72 (and echoing Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2021 FCA 88), the Federal Court of Appeal ruled that: (1) the CRA's August 2021 administrative Guidelines ("Why" and "How") did not eliminate the legal requirement to follow the scientific method under the five-part Northwest Hydraulic test; and (2) proposed expert witnesses who act as advocates or attempt to establish unproved trial facts through the back door of an expert report are properly excluded. Conversely, in recent SME manufacturing and food-science appeals—such as Canafric Inc. v. The King, 2023 TCC 108 and Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. The King (2025)—the Tax Court allowed SR&ED appeals where claimants proved genuine technological uncertainty in specific formulation/processing contexts and maintained contemporaneous records of hypotheses tested and experimental results.

Clarified that while technical constraints in a business context are relevant, economic or cost-efficiency obstacles alone do not constitute technological uncertainty under s. 248(1).
Canafric Inc. v. The King, 2023 TCC 108 & Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. The King (2025)

Confirmed that technological uncertainty can exist even where known ingredients/preservatives are used in a novel context, and that contemporaneous records need only track hypotheses, tests, and results for practitioners skilled in the art.
